Mama was at the stove. She didn't turn around.

"There she is," the man in the chair said. He smiled at Mara the way the preacher smiled at children he didn't know the names of. "Took you long enough."

"The jars were behind the pickles," Mara said. Her voice came out steadier than she expected. "Mama always puts the peaches in back."

"Set them here, honey," Mama said, and there it was again, that word, soft as a warning.

Mara crossed to the counter. Every step, she felt the ledger's hard edge against her ribs, felt the cardigan pulling where her arms held it closed. She put the jar down beside the cutting board and reached for the opener in the drawer, because that was what a girl would do if she'd only gone down for peaches.

"Your mother tells us your grandfather kept his accounts in town," the man said. "At the bank."

Mara twisted the lid. It stuck, then broke loose with a pop that made the man at the window flinch.

"I wouldn't know," she said. "He never let me see his papers."
